question.knowledge_point: Using Alternative Forms of Double-Angle Formula to Simplify Expressions
question.problem: Express $2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})-1$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{5\pi }{3}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})-1 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{10\pi }{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression Using the Alternate Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
question.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x)(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)={sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x
$$

Then, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x)(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=1.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression Using the Alternate Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

Next, we recall the following identity: 

$$
1-{sin}^{2}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x
$$

Using the above identity, we can further simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-(1-{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡x}}{\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡x}}-\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-2{cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1-2{cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Factoring Alternative Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
question.worked_solution:
First, we can simplify our expression by factoring it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{4}⁡x-2{sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{4}⁡x & =({sec}^{2}⁡x)^{2}-2{sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x+({tan}^{2}⁡x)^{2} \\  & ={({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)}^{2} & ={(1)}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{sec}^{4}⁡x-2{sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{4}⁡x=1.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Factoring Alternative Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the following identities: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }
$$

Using the above identity, we can simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }-\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }}\frac{\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta ({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1) & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={tan}^{4}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{csc}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ={tan}^{4}⁡\theta .
$$

question.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Factoring and Using Various Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x+1}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x+1} & =\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot 1+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can use $(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x+1} & =\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x})}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x+1}={cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$

question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify our expression and use again $(2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ({tan}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }({tan}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{\cancel{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }} \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & =({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)-1 \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -2.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically
question.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x={t}^{2}+5,\,\,\,y=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,t\ne 0.
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for ${t}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x={t}^{2}+5\,⇒\,{t}^{2}=x-5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting ${t}^{2}=x-5$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{x-5}\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{1}{x-5}.$

Finally, since $t\ne 0$ and $x={t}^{2}+5,$ we must have $x\ne 5.$ 

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x-5},\,x\ne 5.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically With Trigonometric Functions
question.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{y}{3})}^{2}+{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is ${(\frac{y}{3})}^{2}+{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}=1.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically With Trigonometric Functions
question.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x-3}{5} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\frac{y+2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{x-3}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{y+2}{3})}^{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is ${(\frac{x-3}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{y+2}{3})}^{2}=1.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at the origin?
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

$$

$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
question.problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+3}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+3)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+3)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x+2)^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x+2)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=9.$

question.knowledge_point: Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola Whose Vertex Is at the Origin
question.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and which passes through the point $(-3,-3)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(-3,-3),$ we can substitute $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3=2pt \\ -3=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{3}{2p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =p{(-\frac{3}{2p})}^{2} \\ -3 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{4{p}^{2}} \\ -3 & =\frac{9}{4p} \\ 4p & =-3 \\ p & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(-\frac{3}{4})t,\,y=(-\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=-\frac{3}{2}t,\,y=-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$
